idiom_name: std::variant<...> command payload + std::visit overload set
implementation_notes: The modern C++ default: the command is a closed std::variant of parameter structs, the alternative index is the discriminator the compiler maintains, and std::visit dispatches to an overload set (usually the overload pattern, or a visitor struct with one operator() per command). This replaces the abstract Command base class: the set of operations is a type, exhaustiveness is checked when the visitor covers every alternative, and commands stay value types with no allocation. Serialization is still explicit (nlohmann/json, protobuf, cereal) and must emit a stable tag, because the alternative index is not stable across versions.
pitfalls: std::visit throws std::bad_variant_access on a valueless_by_exception variant; decide that failure policy at the deserialization boundary instead of letting it escape.
A catch-all 'auto&&' overload in the visitor makes new command alternatives compile without a handler, silently losing the exhaustiveness the variant was chosen for.
The alternative index is a compiler detail, not a wire tag: deserialization must map an explicit string tag to the alternative, or a reordered variant misreads old messages.

variants.name: Classic abstract Command hierarchy with virtual execute()
variants.idiom_name: abstract Command + concrete subclasses, tag written by the serializer
variants.implementation_notes: The classic realization kept from the GoF/POEAA lineage: an abstract Command with a virtual execute() and one subclass per operation, dispatched polymorphically on the receiving side. Because the C++ type is not part of the data, the discriminator has to come from outside the object graph - a hand-written type field, protobuf's message type, or a Boost.Serialization class registration plus factory - and a registry rebuilds the concrete type before execute() runs. Choose it when commands are also first-class local objects (undo stacks, macro recording) and the wire form is a secondary concern.
pitfalls: Deserialization needs a factory or class registration that must stay in step with the wire tags; a command type missing from the registry fails only at runtime.
Hand-written polymorphic serialization leaks and drifts from the class hierarchy - use a library that registers the classes, or prefer a value type.
Virtual dispatch means the command owns behavior, so the receiver's dependencies have to be reachable from the object: easy to end up with commands calling into the sender's world.
